New pod live with @clefourrier on the Open LLM Leaderboard V2 and the state of LLM Evaluation!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GSUpDgTW4AAvi8v.jpg
Quoting @swyx
🆕Benchmarks 201 with @clefourrier of the @huggingface Open LLM Leaderboard!
Why Chat Arenas are **OVERRATED**:
- they bias sycophancy/assertiveness over factuality
- annotators are not representative of humanity
- models are argmaxxing public arena data
- not reproducible
- can't give fine grained test of model capabilities
Why you should STOP using LLMs as Judges:
- Position bias (prefer first answers)
- Self bias (prefer their own answers)
- Length bias (prefer long answers)
- Discrete bias (can't do continuous ranges)
- Reproducibility (GPT4 closed source - prefer @seungonekim's Prometheus or @baaibeijing JudgeLM)

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
#博客 为何模型上下文协议 (MCP) 会获胜？[译]
Latent Space 分析了模型上下文协议 (MCP) 快速崛起并有望成为智能体领域主导标准的原因，认为其成功是技术优势、生态支持、品牌效应、协议基础、实践验证和迭代更新等多因素共同作用的结果。
MCP 胜出的主要原因如下：
1. MCP 是旧理念的“AI 原生”版本
- 技术上类似于 OpenAPI 等传统标准，但 MCP 针对 AI 智能体设计，更符合 AI 开发者的需求和习惯，更符合人体工程学。
- 吸取了 Claude Sonnet 在代码能力评测中的成功经验以及构建有效智能体的实践经验，针对智能体开发中反复出现的模式进行了标准化。
- 专注于解决动态上下文接入的核心问题，区别于早期侧重 LLM 互操作性的框架。
- 明确区分了 工具（模型控制）、资源（应用控制）和 提示（用户控制） 三个关键要素，使智能体开发更具结构性和效率。
因此，相对于通用标准如 OpenAPI 和侧重 LLM 互操作性的框架如 LangChain，MCP 更具优势。
2. MCP 是一个拥有强大支持者的“开放标准”
- 大厂（Anthropic）的支持是标准成功的关键因素，相比创业公司主导的标准更易被信任和采用。
- MCP 拥有详细且完善的规范文档，这超越了许多竞争对手，甚至优于 OpenAI 的函数调用文档。
因此，相对于创业公司主导的标准 (如 Composio) 和缺乏完整规范的方案，MCP 更具优势。
3. Anthropic 拥有最佳的开发者 AI 品牌
- 开发者对 Anthropic 的品牌和产品（如 Claude Sonnet）有高度认可和喜爱，这有助于 MCP 的推广和接受度。
- Anthropic 支持更多工具，而 MCP 能够更好地集成和处理大量工具，更符合实际应用需求。
因此，相对于其他公司（如 Cisco）推出的同类标准，Anthropic 的品牌优势为 MCP 带来了更大的成功机会。
4. MCP 基于 LSP (Language Server Protocol) 协议
- MCP 聪明地借鉴了成熟且成功的 LSP 协议，避免了从零开始设计新协议的风险，并利用了 LSP 的既有优势和生态。
- LSP 的 JSON RPC 消息传递机制保证了客户端和服务器之间的高度互操作性。
因此，相对于其他“未经证实”的标准格式，基于 LSP 的 MCP 更可靠、更易于集成和推广。
5. MCP 通过完整的第一方客户端、服务器、工具和 SDK 进行了充分的实践和内部验证
- MCP 发布时就配套提供了 Claude Desktop 客户端、多个服务器参考实现、调试工具 MCP Inspector 和 Claude Desktop DevTools，以及 Python 和 TypeScript SDK。
- 后续又推出了官方 CLI 客户端 Claude Code，进一步体现了 Anthropic 内部对 MCP 的实际应用和验证。
因此，相对于其他公司缺乏充分内部测试和实践的标准 (如 Meta 的 llama-stack)，MCP 更成熟、更可靠。
6. MCP 起步于最小的基础，但会随着路线图持续更新
- MCP 采用了最小化的接口设计，易于理解和上手。
- MCP 保持了快速迭代和更新的节奏，不断增加新功能和完善协议，例如官方 MCP 注册表、远程服务器发现等功能都在快速推进和发布。
因此，相对于其他启动后未能保持势头的标准，MCP 能够持续吸引开发者关注和采用。

The Six Elements of Agent Engineering
compiling answers from @simonw's definitions thread (thanks @lilianweng @ruthefordml @hwchase17 @DanielMiessler @Dan_Jeffries1 @romechenko)
IMPACT:
- Intent (Instructions + Evals)
- Memory (@gneubig reusable workflows)

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
Dharmesh Shah 谈 AI Agent 与未来 - @latentspacepod
Latent Space 播客对话邀请了 Dharmesh Shah，他是 HubSpot 的联合创始人，也是 的创建者。主持人 @FanaHOVA 和 @swyx 共同探讨了 AI Agents、商业模式、未来工作方式等话题。
1. 什么是 AI Agents？
· 定义：Dharmesh 把 AI Agents 描述为“用 AI 驱动的软件，目标是完成某件事”。这个定义很广，从简单工具到能自主规划任务的复杂系统都算在内。
· 演变：他提到 AI Agents 从早期的实验（如 Baby AGI）发展到如今更实用的应用，技术进步让它们更可靠、更强大。
2. 混合团队：人与 AI 合作
· 概念：Dharmesh 提出了“混合团队”的未来愿景——人类和 AI Agents 像队友一样协作。这类似于过去的全职与合同工、办公室与远程工作的混合模式。
· 意义：AI 不再只是工具，而是能分担工作的伙伴，改变职场组织方式。
3. AI 的商业模式
Dharmesh 讨论了两种新兴的商业模式：
· 工作即服务（WaaS）：软件直接完成工作（如审查合同），按工作量收费。
· 结果即服务（RaaS）：按成果收费（如解决客服问题）。
观点：他认为 RaaS 被高估了，因为很多 AI 应用的成果不好衡量，或者价值不一致。比如客服票据的结果容易量化，但设计类任务（如做 logo）的价值因人而异，难以标准化。
4. AI 的记忆功能
· 重要性：Dharmesh 强调 AI 需要持久记忆，尤其是跨智能体的共享记忆。比如，你告诉一个智能体的事情，另一个智能体也应该知道，避免重复输入。
· 未来：他设想一个系统，用户的数据能在不同智能体间共享（用户可控），提升协作效率。
5. 数据隐私与控制
· 挑战：AI 系统需要访问用户数据，但隐私是个大问题。
· 解决方案：Dharmesh 希望用户能像用 OAuth 一样，精细控制哪些数据可以共享给哪些智能体，而不是全盘开放。
6. 标准的作用（如 MCP）
· 什么是 MCP：一种协议，帮助智能体协作、发现彼此并使用工具。
· 价值：Dharmesh 认为 MCP 这样的标准能让多智能体系统更高效，就像互联网靠标准协议连接一样。
7. 软件工程的未来
· AI 的影响：他认为 AI 不会取代工程师，而是增强他们的能力。工程师需要学会与 AI 工具合作。
· 前景：随着 AI 解决更多问题，工程师能创造更大价值，他们的经济价值反而会上升。
8. 域名投资与市场效率
· 兴趣：Dharmesh 喜欢投资域名（如
· 理念：他相信消除市场低效能创造巨大价值，域名交易就是一例。他曾把 卖给 OpenAI，展现了对高效市场的追求。
9. 个人哲学：专注与拒绝
· “抱歉，必须拒绝”：Dharmesh 在博客“Sorry, Must Pass”中写道，他学会了说“不”，以专注重要的事。这源自他对时间有限的认识——说“是”就意味着对其他事说“不”。
· 决策方式：除非是“超级赞同”（hell yes），否则默认拒绝，减少内疚感，保持高效。

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
Just finished listening to a great conversation with @Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder and creator of on the Latent Space podcast hosted by @swyx and @fanahova (@latentspacepod).
His take on AI agents stood out. Here are the 7 points I found most useful 👇
🔹 What is an agent?
"AI-powered software that accomplishes a goal." Then classify by autonomy, determinism, synchronicity, and interaction style.

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
Thought I'd post the takeaways I had from this that I wrote down a bit ago:
-Originally introduced by Hinton in "Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network", the goal of distillation is to transfer knowledge from a larger teacher model to a smaller student model while retaining capabilities.
-This is done because of cost to performance tradeoffs pushing further down the pareto frontier for more practical use cases.
-As @swyx points out, the slope of the pareto frontier essentially maps to the strength of SOTA distillation techniques, becoming less steep as they become better.
-Distillation can create a better model than training a small model on the same data that the large model had, due to the extra information available in the logits of the teacher model compared to the single answer in the dataset.
-Traditional distillation optimizes for minimum KL divergence between the distribution of the teacher model and student model sampling distributions.
-Somewhat counterintuitively, when using synthetic data to improve a model, you can get a better end dataset through compute or cost matched sampling of a small model when finetuning a larger model (this was shown with Gemma 2 9b synthetic data outperforming Gemma 2 27b for finetuning the 27b model)
-Supervised distillation can result in train-inference mismatch where the student model will perform poorly when it finds itself in a token sequence that the teacher model wouldn't have entered at all.
-This problem is dealt with through On Policy Distillation which gets logits from the teacher using samples from the student model and minimizes per-token KL divergence. This was used in Gemma 2 post training.
-On Policy Distillation is derived from using Reverse KL divergence minimization, where you swap the student and teacher distributions and get different results because of scale asymmetry.
-This has been combined with speculative decoding (having a small model generate candidate tokens for a large model to choose from) concepts for Speculative On Policy Distillation where a student models trajectory is corrected by the teacher filling in sampling if it would diverge too much from the teacher's sampling during distillation. This was used to train AI overviews for Google search.
Quoting @latentspacepod

summary:
🆕 SF Compute: Commoditizing Compute
We're excited for our latest deep dive into the compute market with @evanjconrad of @sfcompute!
It should not be normal for the prices of one of the world’s most important resources right now to swing from $8 to $1 per hour (as @picocreator observed) based on drastically inelastic demand AND supply curves - from 3 year lock-in contracts to stupendously competitive over-ordering dynamics for NVIDIA allocations — especially with increasing baseline compute needed for even the simplest academic ML research and for new AI startups getting off the ground.
The entire point of SFC is creating liquidity between GPU owners and consumers and making it broadly tradable, even programmable. As we explore, these are the primitives that you can then use to create your own, high quality, custom GPU availability for your time and money budget, similar to how Amazon Spot Instances automated the selective buying of unused compute.
The ultimate end state of where all this is going is GPU that trade like other perishable, staple commodities of the world - oil, soybeans, milk. Because the contracts and markets are so well established, the price swings also are not nearly as drastic, and people can also start hedging and managing the risk of one of the biggest costs of their business, just like we have risk-managed commodities risks of all other sorts for centuries. As a former derivatives trader, you can bet that swyx doubleclicked on that…
Also to end off, we of course had to ask about how on earth SFCompute manages to have such immaculate vibes....

summary:
Listened to @latentspacepod's most recent podcast with the folks from Claude Code (very good listen, highly recommend) and it gives a lot more insight into Anthropic's priorities when building out Claude Code.
While they do have to consider how to create a great UX, they have a different focus from the AI IDEs like Cursor. Seems like they're focusing more on the bare bones and banking on model improvements eventually making these kinds of optimizations unnecessary. They're also deliberately focusing on making it as simple as possible, which allows anybody to customize it to fit their own needs and compose it with other tools.
So yeah it can be annoying to have to iterate on our own prompts and workflows but it fits with their idea of Claude Code as a "primitive" that developers can shape and build on like they want.
Plus, the bitter lesson... building the thinnest possible layer and riding on model improvements is probably the smartest long-term play, especially for an AI provider like Anthropic.

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
We're witnessing the fastest consolidation in the history of developer tooling.
Seriously, it's never moved this fast before.
Blink, and you might miss another billion-dollar acquisition or the release of yet another AI coding agent.
And here we are, trying to catch breath and make sense of it all. If you're a developer, or even vaguely tech-adjacent, you absolutely need to pay attention, because the implications are massive.
A brief "history" lesson first. Back in February 2025 AD, Anthropic Claude Code research preview, the first notable CLI coding assistant. The tool was smooth, and the model powerful. Recently, on the @latentspacepod podcast (@swyx), they stated that Claude Code wrote around 80–90% of its own code. Talk about bootstrapping on steroids. Today, they have released SDK for devs to build composable coding agent tooling.
Not far behind was OpenAI, which released Codex CLI, a conversational, terminal-based coding assistant that felt magical when it first debuted. (I even forked Codex CLI myself to understand its token usage and workflow, check out my gist if you're curious.) Meanwhile, in the open-source corner, we had Aider. Then Sourcegraph's Amp joined the fray in May, removing its waitlist and allowing anyone to spin up multistep agents with a simple agent(.)md file.
Cursor's trajectory is most fascinating. Originally just another fork of VS Code, Cursor quickly became a developer favorite and is now a SaaS unicorn with a rumored $10 billion valuation. Cursor also shook things up recently by introducing unlimited completions and shifting their MAX model to API-based pricing, subtle moves, sure, but these reflect the reality that foundational model providers are adjusting their pricing strategies as market realities hit, and everyone is still adjusting and competitors are building pressure.
In the middle of this craziness, OpenAI decided it wasn't playing games and threw $3 billion at Windsurf, making clear their intent to dominate developer tooling. Google's latest entry, Jules, they are still keeping me on the waitlist, competing with Codex and Copilot by integrating with GitHub and leveraging ephemeral cloud environments for asynchronous development.
So, what’s the story beneath all this chaos? Here’s where my analyst hat goes on. I see five mega-trends shaping up:
1. The Commoditization of Interfaces
No one cares about IDE loyalty anymore. Seriously, who has time to be loyal when every agent, whether it’s Cursor, Windsurf, or Jules, essentially offers the same basic functionality? Developers hop between tools—I've jumped from Cursor to Windsurf to Claude Code, chasing convenience or a few extra free API calls. UI and UX alone won't save companies; they'll need something deeper to hold developers’ attention.
2. Token Economics & The Coming Crunch
We’re still in the "token-first" world, where every provider optimizes for token consumption because that's their revenue model. Yet, having explored the API calls, I noticed just how aggressively inefficient these tools can be. This inefficiency won’t last. Once subsidies fade and true market prices hit, companies offering smarter, token-efficient solutions will win. The future belongs to the most cost-conscious innovators.
3. Agent Simplicity and Spec-driven Workflows
Here's something wild: almost every agent today is powered by simple plaintext rule files. Think .cursor/rules, CLAUDE(.)md, agent(.)md. Today's "state-of-the-art" agents are basically glorified text lookups against structured specifications. The complexity we see is actually smoke and mirrors. The real challenge—and opportunity—is evolving these basic setups into something more robust and persistent.
4. Memory is the New Frontier
Current AI agents are embarrassingly forgetful. Seriously, every new task rebuilds context from scratch. It's like they have goldfish memory—zero persistence. The next massive leap forward in AI tooling will revolve around intelligent, persistent memory systems. Can your agent remember past interactions, avoid redundant work, and ground new tasks in existing knowledge? Whoever solves this elegantly will dominate the next wave. :wink-wink:
5. The Flywheel Effect & Incumbent Domination
OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google—the foundational giants—are spinning up data centers at unprecedented scales, optimizing for margins. This creates a flywheel effect: each improvement fuels more user adoption, more feedback, and even greater market dominance. Jeff Bezos famously said, "Your margin is my opportunity." The biggest players are living this motto right now, making it exceedingly hard for smaller entrants to compete directly.
So, where will we be next year?
I predict an intensified battle around memory persistence, token efficiency, and more than spec-driven automation. In order to reach general adoption, tools that intelligently reuse context, minimize API overhead, and streamline spec-to-code workflows that bring in observability will explode in popularity. Meanwhile, smaller or niche tools will struggle unless they offer significant breakthroughs in memory management or ultra-specific domain expertise.
> Bottom line: We're at an inflection point. Developers have never had it so good, yet the stakes have never been higher. Those who adapt quickly—embracing efficiency, innovation in memory systems, and smarter token consumption—will shape the next steps.
Blink again, and the entire landscape could shift.

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
AI 软件工程智能体（SWE Agents）的快速发展和对行业的影响，来自 @latentspacepod 分享
SWE 智能体成本低，效率高：
OpenAI Codex 和 Google Jules 等 AI 编码智能体推出后，定价策略非常激进——Codex 每60秒可免费发起一次请求，Jules 也有类似的无额外费用模式。这种“成本低到几乎免费”的趋势让小团队能够以极低的成本实现高效率，产生“收入（ARR）比员工数量多”的现象。例如，Cognition、Bolt 等公司已经实现了这一目标。
数据战争（Token Data War）：
AI 模型需要高质量数据来提升性能，而传统数据来源（如 GitHub）已不够用。文章指出，当前的竞争焦点在于获取用户的使用数据。像 LMArena 这样的公司通过1000万美元的种子轮融资，免费提供推理服务来吸引用户，目的是收集数据。这种模式甚至可能演变为“用户使用 AI 还会被付费”的新趋势。
小团队崛起（Tiny Teams）：
强调 “Tiny Teams” 是 AI 工程师生产力的体现，这些团队通常只有少数成员，但借助 SWE 智能体能实现高盈利和高效率。相比之下，“Vibe Coding” 被认为效率较低。小型团队被视为“一人独角兽”的更现实版本，未来可能带来更多成功案例。
市场演变与商业模式：
SWE 智能体市场经历了几个阶段：从 Copilot 的固定收费，到 Codeium 的免费消费者版+企业收费，再到 Devin 的高端收费模式，再到 Bolt 等面向非编码者的扩展。现在，Codex 和 Jules 通过免费或低价模式获取用户数据，进一步推动了模型改进。这种模式下，数据价值远超直接收入，像 Perplexity（估值140亿美元）和 Cursor（90亿美元）这样的公司尽管利润为负，仍因数据价值获得高估值。
未来趋势与活动：
AI Engineer World’s Fair 活动，Gamma、Bolt 等公司将在 “Tiny Teams” 主题下展示成果，Codex 和 Jules 的负责人也将参与。此外，作者呼吁参与者加入 Hackathon 并填写 AI 工程状态调查。
总结：
AI 编码智能体的低成本和高效率正在重塑行业，小型团队因此崛起。同时，数据成为 AI 竞争的核心，市场模式从收费转向免费甚至补贴用户以换取数据。这篇文章揭示了 AI 技术如何通过降低成本和提升生产力，推动新的商业模式和团队形态的出现。

went from frying chicken during the pandemic to getting picked for Maven 100. and honestly it still blows my mind.
I had been working in restaurants for 7 years when the pandemic hit and I decided I needed to do something different with my life.
I taught myself how to code through the pandemic. Long hours spent on google and youtube. I was writing every week about whatever technical concepts I could learn. I was spinning up websites for local restaurants free of charge.
And I was also DM'ing people in tech since I had absolutely no network whatsoever. That's actually how I met @swyx who I now consider a close friend, and have the honor of co-teaching this cohort with.
He had just released the @Coding_Career book that I found and just cold emailed him asking for the book, because I couldn't afford to pay him.
many years later I have 5x'd my income from being below the poverty line to the 1% of earners for my age bracket.
Anyways, needless to say that I'm eternally grateful to my past-self for putting in the hard work. That has put me in the position to teach others the same hard-skills that I developed over the pandemic, in hopes that I can help other people change their lives through the information in AI that I now know.
And throughout the entire teaching process, @MavenHQ has been a fantastic partner, and I'd highly recommend anyone thinking about teaching a live-cohort-based course to consider them.

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
This was a solid listen from @latentspacepod w/ severe; key ideas, @polynoamial emphasized that the recent advances from OpenAI (the o-series reasoning models, Deep Research, Reinforcement Fine-Tuning) signal a decisive shift from training-time scaling to test-time compute (TTC): giving an already-capable base model minutes-to-hours of “deliberation” reliably beats simply making the network larger.
The podcast crystallizes 4 key ideas:
1/ Emergent reasoning only appears once System-1 competence (pre-train scale) crosses a threshold
2/ TTC scales along a cost wall (energy/$) & a clock-time wall (iteration speed)
3/ Self-play and multi-agent RL are far harder outside two-player zero-sum games, requiring new objective functions
4/ Evaluation & alignment must evolve away from multiple-choice tests toward open-ended benchmarks
For founders, builders & investors, the opportunity now seems to lie in “reasoning infrastructure”: TTC-efficient runtimes, agent orchestration, eval stacks & domain-specific data loops

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
“A lot of software will become partially autonomous”
One of my favorite highlights from @karpathy’s talk is talking about how to make the agent “generation-verification” loop go as fast as possible.
IMO the nuance is whether the agent is solving tasks on behalf of the user or assisting the user with information 💡👇
1️⃣ Have the agent solve tasks on behalf of the user: these are routine tasks that the user just wants to offload, like summarizing a research report, processing invoices, redlining contracts. The agent needs to be constrained to solve the task well. This is directly related to the “automation UX” I talked about in my talks.
The human doesn’t necessarily learn things here. They just need to supervise outputs to make sure they’re correct. They don’t need to be in the loop at every step of the process.
2️⃣Have the agent provide information to the user: this is what every deep research UX is about. The tasks is more open-ended, dependent on the user input, and how useful this is is constrained by the user’s own brain clockspeed.
The optimal UX here involves providing as much useful information in a way that’s also the easiest to consume, and lets the user iterate as fast as possible.
Credits to @latentspacepod article for the image below. The second image is from my own talk.
Kaparthy’s talk:
My slides from the world fair:

📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GuEizCpWcAALy0Q.jpg
Quoting @karpathy
Nice - my AI startup school talk is now up! Chapters:
0:00 Imo fair to say that software is changing quite fundamentally again. LLMs are a new kind of computer, and you program them *in English*. Hence I think they are well deserving of a major version upgrade in terms of software.
6:06 LLMs have properties of utilities, of fabs, and of operating systems => New LLM OS, fabbed by labs, and distributed like utilities (for now). Many historical analogies apply - imo we are computing circa ~1960s.
14:39 LLM psychology: LLMs = "people spirits", stochastic simulations of people, where the simulator is an autoregressive Transformer. Since they are trained on human data, they have a kind of emergent psychology, and are simultaneously superhuman in some ways, but also fallible in many others. Given this, how do we productively work with them hand in hand?
Switching gears to opportunities...
18:16 LLMs are "people spirits" => can build partially autonomous products.
29:05 LLMs are programmed in English => make software highly accessible! (yes, vibe coding)
33:36 LLMs are new primary consumer/manipulator of digital information (adding to GUIs/humans and APIs/programs) => Build for agents!
Thank you again for the invite @ycombinator and congrats again on an awesome events! I'll post some links/references in the reply.

summary:
Love listening to OpenAI researchers (and Altman) because they often hint at what's coming, even by REFUSING to answer questions. From this episode with Noam Brown, we can infer that:
1️⃣ Improved multi-agent capabilities and longer horizon reasoning are coming soon. I think GPT-5 will be a step, perhaps modest, in these directions. Brown says they'll share more "in the not too distant future." We're expecting GPT-5 this summer.
2️⃣ Their approach to building world models is Bitter Pill influenced. Brown thinks world models emerge with scale, including the ability to distinguish agents from other aspects of the world model.
3️⃣ Diffusion may have a role in reasoning. This was perhaps the biggest seeming admission by omission. Asked directly about diffusion's possible role in reasoning, he refused to answer.
Great episode if you're interested in reasoning, and where it's taking us with long horizon tasks and multi-agent systems.

summary:
Congrats to the @pratikbhavsar and team for launching the Agent Leaderboard v2!
We caught up in a special lightning pod to discuss the leaderboard and how it is challenging to evaluate base LLMs for agents now that most models can do basic function calling:
We now care about multiturn, dynamic personas, domain specific tools across 5 domains: banking, healthcare, investment, telecom, and insurance.
Overall, GPT4.1 is the best generalist agent model and 4.1 mini is the most cost efficient. a nice result for @openai!
Quoting @rungalileo
Our Agent Leaderboard v2 is LIVE: We’ve added more models, a second benchmark, and more complexity to reflect the evolution of multi-agent systems. What LLMs came out on top?
Agent Leaderboard v2 is our next step in benchmarking AI agents by moving beyond tool-calling tests to realistic enterprise scenarios. We simulated real customer support conversations across five industries with multi-turn dialogues, complex decision-making, and interdependent goals.
Our evaluation focuses on two of our key agent metrics:
- Action Completion: Did the agent fully accomplish the user’s goals, with explicit confirmations?
- Tool Selection Quality: How effectively does the agent choose and use tools in context?
Here were the key takeaways as of today 🧵

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
Cline 官宣 $32m Seed+A 轮融资：用“计划+行动”革新编码，抛弃 RAG，非编码工作流 —— @latentspacepod 对 @sdrzn & @pashmerepat 的深度访谈
1. Cline 是什么？为什么这么火？
@cline 是一个 AI 驱动的编码助手，装在 VS Code、Cursor 等编辑器里，像一个超级聪明的“程序员搭档”。你可以用自然语言告诉它想做什么，比如“帮我写个网页”或“修复这个bug”，它就会自动去读代码、改文件、跑命令，甚至还能连外部工具（像 GitHub、Slack）。它开源、免费，6个月内下载量接近200万，火爆的原因有几个：
· 简单好用：直接装在 VS Code 里，不用装新软件，开发者上手快
· 开源透明：代码公开，用户可以自己改，还能带自己的 API Key，不用担心数据隐私
· 功能强大：不仅能写代码，还能干非编码的事，比如自动发社交媒体帖子、做 PPT，吸引了非程序员用户
· 社区支持：有6000多个 fork，开发者们基于 Cline 造出各种新玩法，社区活跃
2. “计划+行动”模式：Cline 的创新
传统 AI 编码工具（像 Copilot）主要是“问答式”，你问一句，它答一句，适合小修小补。Cline 提出了“计划+行动”（Plan & Act）模式，彻底改变了工作流：
· 计划模式：AI 先跟你聊清楚需求，探索代码库，列出详细的修改计划。比如你要加个新功能，它会先问：“页面长啥样？需要哪些文件？”然后生成一个清晰的方案
· 行动模式：确认计划后，AI 就开干，自动改代码、跑测试、提交 PR。你可以全程盯着，或者喝杯咖啡让它自己搞定。
这种模式让 AI 更像一个有条理的“队友”，而不是只会补代码的工具。文章提到，很多用户自己摸索出了类似流程，Cline 就把这套方法做成了产品功能，降低了使用门槛。
3. 为什么抛弃 RAG，拥抱“上下文工程”？
RAG 是过去 AI 编码的常见技术，通过索引代码库，快速找到相关片段传递给模型。但 Cline 团队认为 RAG 已经过时，原因有三：
· 不精准：RAG 把代码切成小块，丢进向量数据库，检索时容易丢上下文，模型理解不完整，生成的代码可能有 bug
· 复杂且低效：维护 RAG 系统需要额外基础设施，模型还得处理乱七八糟的代码片段，容易“精神分裂”
· 模型进步快：现在的 AI（像 Claude 3.5）能直接处理超长上下文（比如 200K token），完全可以直接读整个代码库，不需要 RAG 的“取巧”
Cline 应用了“上下文工程”（Context Engineering），核心是让 AI 像人类程序员一样主动探索代码库，智能管理上下文。主要包括：
· 动态上下文管理：AI 实时读取和总结文件，保持上下文最新、不冗余
· AST 分析：用抽象语法树（AST）精准定位代码结构，比如找到某个函数或类
· 叙事完整性：像讲故事一样，确保 AI 在长期任务中记得前因后果，不跑偏
· 记忆库：自动保存开发者的偏好和项目“部落知识”（没写进文档的经验），让 AI 更懂你
这套方法让 Cline 在复杂任务上表现更好，比如改大型代码库或处理多文件联动。
4. MCP：Cline 的“超级连接器”
MCP 是 Cline 的杀手锏，让它能连接各种外部工具和服务，干更多事。Cline 很早就支持 MCP，还推出了自己的 MCP 市场，类似“插件商店”。热门 MCP 包括：
· 文件系统 MCP：管理文件和目录
· 浏览器自动化：用 Playwright、Puppeteer 控制浏览器，适合爬网页或测试
· Git 工具：直接在 Cline 里提交代码、关 issue
· 文档检索：快速查编程库文档
· 第三方集成：连 Slack 发消息、用 Perplexity 查资料，甚至在 Unity 里做 3D 建模或用 Ableton 做音乐
MCP 的意外收获是吸引了非程序员。比如，有人用 Cline 自动从 Reddit 抓内容，发到 X；还有人用语音笔记让 Cline 生成专业 PPT。这种“跨界”用法让 Cline 成了一个通用的自动化平台，而不只是编码工具。
5. 非编码用例：Cline 的意外惊喜
虽然 Cline 主打编码，但它的 MCP 和自然语言交互让非技术用户也能用。比如：
· 营销自动化：用 Reddit 和 X 的 MCP，抓内容、生成帖子，全程不用写代码
· PPT 生成：用户录一段语音，Cline 用 SlideDev 自动生成漂亮的 PPT
这些案例说明，Cline 的“Agent”能力超出了编码范畴，成了一个能连接各种工具、自动化工作流的平台。
6. 商业模式：开源+企业版
Cline 目前开源免费，用户带自己的 API Key，推理成本直接付给模型提供商。Cline 不赚推理的钱，保持透明，赢得了开发者信任。
那他们怎么赚钱？答案是企业版。很多大公司（包括财富500强）的程序员已经在用 Cline，但企业需要更多控制，比如：
· 统一管理 API Key：避免员工乱用密钥，控制成本
· 安全和隐私：确保代码不外泄，符合企业合规要求
· ROI 证明：提供数据（比如节省的代码行数或时间），帮内部推 AI 工具的人证明价值
Cline 的开源模式降低了企业试用的门槛，很多公司主动找上门，要求定制企业版功能。未来，他们可能会推出类似“内部路由器”的自托管方案，让企业完全掌控数据。
7. 挑战与未来
· MCP 生态的安全性：MCP 像插件，社区贡献的 MCP 可能有恶意代码。Cline 需要更好的审核机制
· 竞争激烈：有6000多个 Cline fork，甚至三星都 fork 了 Cline 做内部版。市场还有其他玩家，像 Cursor、Cloud Code
· 模型成本下降：如果 AI 模型推理成本趋近于零（比如 Google 免费开放 Gemini），Cline 的“带你自己的密钥”模式可能需要调整
未来，Cline 想做“Agent 基础设施”的领导者，不仅限于 VS Code，还要扩展到 CLI、JetBrains，甚至非开发场景（像智能车、冰箱）。他们计划推出 SDK，让开发者基于 Cline 建自己的 Agent，目标是定义未来10年的编程范式。
8. 一些有趣的细节
· “快应用”被淘汰：Cursor 曾用小模型修补大模型的代码修改（叫 Fast Apply），但随着大模型进步，这种复杂方案已没必要。Cline 坚持用单一强大模型，简单高效
· RAG 被吐槽：Cline 团队认为 RAG 像“精神分裂”，不如让模型直接读完整代码库。他们管 RAG 叫“思维病毒”
· Cline 的人格化：Cline 被赋予了“他/他”的代词，像个“酷酷的小伙子”，用户觉得更有亲切感，信任度更高
· 社区与 fork：Cline的6000个 fork 既是挑战（有人拿去融资）也是机遇（社区贡献新想法）。团队心态开放，觉得“抄就抄，我们是领头羊”

This IS a big deal. Wonderful to see a strong open model from the US.
As covered in last week’s @latentspacepod LLM Paper Club, Subliminal Learning ramifications seem profound & frankly the Chinese open models have been the best.
Now hopefully Sovereign AI efforts for the rest.
Quoting @sama
gpt-oss is a big deal; it is a state-of-the-art open-weights reasoning model, with strong real-world performance comparable to o4-mini, that you can run locally on your own computer (or phone with the smaller size). We believe this is the best and most usable open model in the world.
We're excited to make this model, the result of billions of dollars of research, available to the world to get AI into the hands of the most people possible. We believe far more good than bad will come from it; for example, gpt-oss-120b performs about as well as o3 on challenging health issues. We have worked hard to mitigate the most serious safety issues, especially around biosecurity. gpt-oss models perform comparably to our frontier models on internal safety benchmarks.
We believe in individual empowerment. Although we believe most people will want to use a convenient service like ChatGPT, people should be able to directly control and modify their own AI when they need to, and the privacy benefits are obvious.
As part of this, we are quite hopeful that this release will enable new kinds of research and the creation of new kinds of products. We expect a meaningful uptick in the rate of innovation in our field, and for many more people to do important work than were able to before.
OpenAI’s mission is to ensure AGI that benefits all of humanity. To that end, we are excited for the world to be building on an open AI stack created in the United States, based on democratic values, available for free to all and for wide benefit.

@latentspacepod 分享了 GPT-5 一个关键变更：AI 开始从 「使用工具」进化到了「以工具思考」。
- 旧模式：使用工具（Use Tools）。 过去，模型像一个调度员。它理解任务，然后调用一个预设的工具（如 get_weather()），拿到结果，再整合进回答。工具是外部的、被动的。
- 新模式：以工具思考（Thinks with them）。 GPT-5 将工具内化为了其思维过程的一部分。它不再是调用一下然后回复，而是像人类一样，主动地、迭代地、探索性地使用工具来构建认知和解决方案。

summary:
@latentspacepod 的第三篇文章评测了 GPT-5 的视觉理解能力，结论是 GPT-5 在简单视觉任务上略有提升，但核心短板仍在。
在如 Vision Checkup 这样的通用视觉排行榜上，GPT-5 表现优异，名列前茅。这主要归功于其强大的推理能力，能「更深入地思考它所看到的东西」。
在更专业的、要求精确定位的 RF100-VL 基准测试中，GPT-5 表现极差，其 mAP 分数（1.5）远低于 Gemini 2.5 Pro（13.3）。
文章认为问题的根源在于「理解≠定位」，GPT-5 能够很好地理解图像内容（例如，识别出图像中有球和防守队员），但无法精确地定位这些物体（即画出准确的边界框）。作者推测，可能是因为其预训练数据中缺乏目标检测相关的任务。

文章认为，GPT-5 真正的突破并非单个模型的能力，而是其模型混合（Mixture of Models）的系统架构，其核心是一个智能路由器。这使得 OpenAI 首次在「每美元所能获得的智能（intelligence per dollar）」这一关键前沿上占据主导地位。
如果说从 GPT-3 到 GPT-4 的突破是专家混合（MoE），那么从 GPT-4o 到 GPT-5 的突破就是模型混合（MoM）。这种架构可以将不同部分（如快速模型和推理模型）独立进行优化和迭代，是一种清晰、可工程化的进步路径，而非神秘的黑魔法。

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
When @MistralAI released their Mixture of Experts (MoE) model, we had a lot of discussions at meli about the performance gains this architecture brought. As the article points out, GPT-4 showed that MoE could make a real difference, proving the leap in performance from GPT-3.
After that, we started asking: what if we could do something similar, but route externally across multiple models? We began experimenting with using an ML model to decide which LLM to call, based on metadata, features, and heuristics. We ran some experiments on RouteLLM.
One clear insight: routing between a strong and a weak model can reduce costs while maintaining the strong model’s performance.
Months ago, I discussed this with @fpingham and @tomas_hk . In March, during his @notdiamond_ai keynote at Tomas was clear about “intelligent model routing” and his vision that the future is multi-model. I remember asking him: will we see providers launch their own model routing this year?
Since then, we’ve seen several ideas, like “auto” modes in IDEs such as @cursor_ai . And now, with @OpenAI 's latest moves, it finally seems to be becoming real.
The future is routing: models, tools, tokens, and imo, prompt optimization at the core of the stack.
Thank you, @swyx @latentspacepod for the article!!

I watch the podcast @latentspacepod with Greg and take some notes:
1/ GPT-4 showed emergent conversational skills but was unreliable. The fix? Reinforcement Learning (RL)—a core OpenAI strength—to validate the model's reasoning against real-world feedback.
2/ Moving away from a static model training to a dynamic "inference-training loop." Models now learn continuously from the data they generate via RL, a fundamental shift to online learning where compute is the primary fuel for intelligence.
3/ GPT-5's defining feature is a leap in "intelligence." It reliably solves complex problems where GPT-4 struggled, achieving top-tier human performance in fields like International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) proofs. It’s about depth, not just breadth.
4/ How to Collaborate with AI:
- Be a manager, not just a user
- Decompose large tasks into smaller, parallel ones.
- Treat it like a colleague: An observable one you can direct precisely.
- Push its limits: Start simple and scale up complexity to understand its true capabilities.
5/ The "Why" of Open Source & a Final Thought:
• Strategy: Open source creates ecosystem dependency, solidifying a tech stack centered on OpenAI and US leadership.
• Inspiration: The number of important problems to solve grows over time. This AI-driven era is a new beginning, not an end.

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
OpenAI’s Router feels like a temporary band-aid on the path to “general purpose adaptive compute”
the question is: “how much compute should I spend for a given query?”
“easier” queries should obv use less compute than complex queries (ex: requires lots of steps to answer). but what do we mean by more/less compute?
there’s a few classes of approaches to consider:
1. Router Approach: Take the request, classify it, and have a smaller model answer it if it’s an easy question. Smaller models mean less parameters so less compute spent.
2. Inference Time Scaling: For reasoning models, do less thinking/tool calling when a question is easy. No need to “think” for 30 seconds to answer what is the capital of France. For this, models need to be trained to use an appropriate amount of inference compute or they can be built into a system which automatically sets and truncates thinking via “thinking budgets” based on the user query
3. Single Model, Dynamic Compute in Forward Pass: these are an under explored class of methods like Matformer (which powers Gemini 3n). The idea is that you can have a single model but in the forward pass you select smaller subsets of parameters to do inference. Effectively this is an inference time way to extract a smaller model for inference from the original model. Commonly you extract this model offline but there’s research to do this based on query hardness.
There’s a great podcast from @latentspacepod with @polynoamial where they discuss that eventually we probably don’t have routers or harnesses as models scale but they’re rlly useful for product builders until we reach those model capabilities
the area I’m most excited about is a mix of 2/3. that’s a world where models are better trained to do appropriate amounts of inference time scaling (in today’s paradigm that means how many tokens to emit during thinking or during its think/tool call loop). At the same time, there’s tons of research left to do in straight up “do less compute in the forward pass itself”. The problem of online dynamic subnetwork extraction from a single model seems sort of utopian, you have a single model and we have a system to decide how much compute to use in the forward step.
my bet is that in the near term we use routers a lot but quickly get very good at inference time scaling appropriately mapped to difficulty. While dynamic compute at the model forward pass level will take more than a year to reach the frontier model scale
for those in this space, along with Noam, another great follow is @adityakusupati who pioneered the matryoshka methods used in Gemini3n

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
RAG 已死，上下文工程为王 —— 来自 Chroma 创始人 @jeffreyhuber 的观点 —— 揭示了 RAG 的局限性并提出了上下文工程作为 AI 应用开发的核心方法。结合技术洞见和创业哲学，强调了精准检索、上下文优化和高质量数据集的重要性。
背景与核心观点
围绕 AI 应用中的信息检索和上下文管理展开，聚焦于 RAG 的局限性以及新兴的“上下文工程”的重要性。Jeff 认为，传统的 RAG 方法已经不足以应对现代 AI 应用的复杂需求，尤其是在上下文窗口越来越长、AI 从简单聊天机器人转向更具影响力的智能体的背景下。他提出，上下文工程——即如何精准、高效地为 AI 模型提供合适的信息——是构建可靠 AI 系统的关键。
为什么“RAG 已死”？
1. RAG 的局限性：
· RAG 这个术语过于宽泛，混淆了检索（Retrieval）、增强（Augmentation）和生成（Generation）三个不同概念，导致开发者难以清晰理解和优化。
· 传统 RAG 通常依赖单一的密集向量搜索，但这在处理复杂任务或大规模数据时效果有限。
· 随着上下文窗口的扩展（例如从几千到百万个 token），模型的注意力机制会衰减（称为“上下文腐烂”，Context Rot），导致性能下降。简单堆砌信息不再有效。
2. 上下文工程的崛起：
· 上下文工程的核心是为每次生成选择最相关的上下文信息，而不是一股脑塞入所有可能相关的数据。
· 它包括两个层面：
· 内循环：为当前生成任务选择合适的上下文。
· 外循环：通过持续优化（例如错误分析、重新分块、调整过滤器）提升上下文选择的质量。
· Jeff 强调，上下文工程不仅是技术问题，还是一种高价值的工程实践，决定了 AI 应用的成败。
上下文工程的五个实用建议
Jeff 提出了五个实用的检索优化建议，帮助开发者构建更高效的 AI 系统：
1. 不要只做“RAG”，而是聚焦于“检索”：
明确区分检索的各个基本操作（密集搜索、词法搜索、过滤、重新排序、上下文组装、评估循环），以便更系统地优化。
2. 混合召回（Hybrid Recall）：
使用向量搜索、词法搜索（regex）和元数据过滤结合的方式，从大量候选数据中筛选出200-300个候选结果，交给 LLM 处理。
3. 重新排序（Re-rank）：
在组装上下文之前，使用 LLM 或专门的重新排序模型（cross-encoder）对候选结果进行精细排序，选出最相关的20-40个。
4. 应对上下文腐烂：
保持上下文紧凑和结构化，避免塞入过多的无关信息。研究表明，上下文越长，模型的注意力分配越差，性能下降。
5. 建立小型高质量数据集（Gold Set）：
花一个晚上，组织团队手动标注一个小型的“查询-上下文”数据集，集成到 CI 和仪表板中，用于评估和优化检索系统。
上下文工程的具体流程
1. 数据摄入（Ingest）：
· 解析与分块：根据领域知识（例如标题、代码块、表格）对数据进行智能分块。
· 丰富数据：添加标题、锚点、符号、元数据等信息。
· 可选：生成摘要：用LLM为代码或API生成自然语言摘要，增强语义理解。
· 嵌入与存储：生成密集向量嵌入，可选加入稀疏信号，存储到数据库。
2. 查询（Query）：
· 第一阶段混合检索：结合向量搜索、词法搜索和元数据过滤，筛选出100-300个候选。
· 重新排序：用LLM或专用模型精选20-40个最相关结果。
· 上下文组装：
· 优先放置指令/系统提示。
· 去重或合并近似内容。
· 确保来源多样性。
· 设置严格的token上限。
3. 外循环（Outer Loop）：
· 缓存与成本控制：优化性能和成本。
· 生成性基准测试：基于小型高质量数据集评估系统表现。
· 错误分析：根据反馈调整分块策略、过滤器或重新排序提示。
· 记忆与压缩：将交互记录总结为可检索的事实，优化长期记忆。
Chroma 发布了两个重要技术报告：
1. Context Rot Technical Report：
揭示了长上下文窗口导致模型性能下降的问题，挑战了 "needle-in-a-haystack" 基准的营销宣传，强调上下文质量的重要性。
2. Generative Benchmarking Technical Report：
提出了一种方法，让 LLM 从数据块生成高质量查询，构建“查询-上下文”数据集，用于评估和优化检索系统。
关于记忆与 AI 的未来
Jeff 认为，“记忆”是上下文工程的直接收益。AI 的记忆能力类似于人类通过学习和反馈不断改进任务表现的能力。上下文工程通过优化上下文选择，让 AI 能够“记住”最相关的信息，从而提升性能。他还预测，未来的检索系统可能：
· 保持在潜在空间（Latent Space）：不依赖自然语言，直接传递嵌入向量。
· 持续检索：而不是一次检索后生成所有内容，AI 可能在生成过程中动态检索。
· 高效内存管理：借鉴数据库中的压缩技术，AI 可能通过离线计算优化记忆结构。
关于 Chroma 的创业哲学
· 专注与耐心：Chroma 选择不追逐短期炒作，而是专注于打造极致的开发者体验，即使这意味着推迟产品发布（如Chroma Cloud）。
· 文化与品牌：公司文化直接影响产品，Chroma 强调一致性与用心，从办公室设计到 API 体验都体现深思熟虑。
· 招聘与愿景：Chroma 招聘注重与公司愿景高度契合的人才，尤其看重对分布式系统、Rust 编程和开发者工具的热情。
· 宗教与价值观：杰夫提到，他对基督教的信仰影响了他对“影响深远”工作的追求，强调为人类福祉而非短期利益做事 -- Amen！

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
I just viewed the podcast from @latentspacepod with Jeff Huber of Chroma and take some quick notes :
1/
What Chroma is (today): evolved from a pip‑installable single‑node vector DB to a modern retrieval engine for AI—Rust, fully multi‑tenant, storage/compute separation, usage‑based pricing, zero‑config DX.
2/
Why retrieval for AI ≠ classic search: humans parse 10 blue links; models can ingest far more. The consumer is the LLM, so you optimize for token budgets, relevance at scale, and tail latency—not CTR.
3/
Context engineering = picking the minimum, most relevant info for the context window—per generation (inner loop) and across time (outer loop). It matters because context rot is real: attention/reasoning degrade as tokens rise.
4/
Hot take: a stable 60k‑token model with sharp attention beats a marketing‑only “5M‑token” window that ignores instructions. Long context ≠ usable context.
5/
Working pattern: two‑stage retrieval. (1) Coarse recall: vector + full‑text/BM25 + metadata → hundreds. (2) LLM re‑ranking → tens. Cost is lower than you think (reports of ~$0.01/1M input tokens with tiny re‑rankers); tail‑latency & API reliability are the hurdles.
6/
Trendl ine: as LLMs get cheaper/faster, brute‑force re‑ranking wins. Next up: continual retrieval (pull evidence mid‑generation) and staying in embedding space.
7/
Code search reality: regex still answers ~85–90% of queries. Embeddings add a steady +5–15% uplift. The winning stack uses both, not either/or.
8/
What Chroma adds for code: native high‑speed regex (single‑node & distributed) + index forking (<100ms clone) so you can version by commit/branch/release and search diffs cheaply.
9/
Indexing principle: write‑time sacrifice for read‑time speed. Tiny corpora? Don’t over‑index. At scale, index aggressively.
10/
Ingestion > query: rewrite chunks (e.g., LLM describes a function in NL; embed code and description as separate indexes), extract rich metadata, and use task‑aware chunking. Front‑load signal so queries are fast and precise.
11/
Measure or it didn’t happen: Generative Benchmarking. Use an LLM to create query↔chunk golden sets from your corpus; track recall/precision vs cost, latency, and API reliability as you iterate.
12/
You don’t need millions of labels. A few hundred high‑quality examples can move mountains. Run a pizza‑powered labeling session; build your eval set; then ship.
13/
Memory, demystified: it’s just better context scheduling. Offline compaction (merge/split/rewrite/re‑index), continuous retrieval, and feedback signals decide what to keep and when to surface it. Skip the slot‑machine acronym soup.
14/
Model marketing vs reality: “needle‑in‑a‑haystack” plots make great slides; builders need honesty about failure modes. Leaderboards ≠ reliable systems.
15/
Chroma’s product stance: teach developers, don’t mystify them. Single focus, slow hiring, craft over hype. Brand coherence (API, docs, office) is part of the engineering standard.
16/
Playbook (1/2):
Default to two‑stage retrieval + monitor P95/P99
Build & use a golden eval set
Structure at ingest
Regex‑first for code; embeddings for the last mile
Forked, versioned indexes
Consider continual retrieval.
17/
Playbook (2/2):
7) Treat re‑ranking as a cheap primitive
8) Choose models for stable attention, not headline context length
9) Prefer serverless, usage‑based infra so your time goes to data & eval, not ops.
18/
Forward look: embedding‑space retrieval, continual retrieval, and (longer‑term) GPU memory paging will raise the ceiling. But the cap today is context engineering. Do less magic, more engineering.

Quoting @latentspacepod
🆕 The new Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Computer Use, and Building SOTA Agents
with @ErikSchluntz, our first @AnthropicAI guest!
---
The vibe shift we observed in July - in favor of Claude 3.5 Sonnet, first introduced in June — has been remarkably long lived and persistent, surviving multiple subsequent updates of 4o, o1 and Gemini versions, for Anthropic’s Claude to end 2024 as the preferred model for AI Engineers and even being the exclusive choice for new code agents like Bolt (our next guest on the pod!), which unlocked so much performance from Claude Sonnet that it went from $0 to $4m ARR in 4 weeks when it launched last month1.
This was even before the bombshell October update of Claude 3.5 Sonnet (and Haiku), making significant improvements in performance over its predecessors:
## Solving SWE-Bench
As part of the October Sonnet release, Anthropic teased a blink-and-you’ll miss it result:
> The updated Claude 3.5 Sonnet shows wide-ranging improvements on industry benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in agentic coding and tool use tasks. On coding, it improves performance on SWE-bench Verified from 33.4% to 49.0%, scoring higher than all publicly available models—including reasoning models like OpenAI o1-preview and specialized systems designed for agentic coding. It also improves performance on TAU-bench, an agentic tool use task, from 62.6% to 69.2% in the retail domain, and from 36.0% to 46.0% in the more challenging airline domain. The new Claude 3.5 Sonnet offers these advancements at the same price and speed as its predecessor.
This was followed up by a blogpost a week later from today’s guest, Erik Schluntz, the engineer who implemented and scored this SOTA2 result using a simple, non-overengineered version of the SWE-Agent framework (you can see the submissions here). We have previously covered the SWE-Bench story extensively:
- Speaking with @jyangballin at ICLR
- Speaking with @AlistairPullen , the previous SOTA (43.8%) on SWEBench Verified (with brief update at DevDay 2024)
- Speaking with @ShunyuYao12 on SWEBench and the ReAct paradigm driving SWE-Agent
One of the notable inclusions in this blogpost are the tools that Erik decided to give Claude, e.g. the “Edit Tool” (h/t @antonosika)
## Claude Computer Use
Because it is one of the best received AI releases of the year, we recommend watching the 2 minute Computer Use intro (and related demos) in its entirety:
Eric also worked on Claude’s function calling, tool use, and computer use APIs, so we discuss that in the episode.
> Erik [00:53:39]: With computer use, just give the thing a browser that's logged into what you want to integrate with, and it's going to work immediately. And I see that reduction in friction as being incredibly exciting. Imagine a customer support team where, okay, hey, you got this customer support bot, but you need to go integrate it with all these things. And you don't have any engineers on your customer support team. But if you can just give the thing a browser that's logged into your systems that you need it to have access to, now, suddenly, in one day, you could be up and rolling with a fully integrated customer service bot that could go do all the actions you care about. So I think that's the most exciting thing for me about computer use, is reducing that friction of integrations to almost zero.
As you’ll see, this is very top of mind for Erik as a former Robotics founder who’s company basically used robots to interface with human physical systems like elevators.

I just watched the newest podcast from @latentspacepod with Ari Morcos from Datology.
Here are my key takeaways
1/ Datology's mission is to automate and simplify data curation for machine learning, making state-of-the-art data accessible to everyone.
2/ The "bitter lesson" from Ari Morcos's research is that data quality is paramount, often more so than model architectures or inductive biases.
3/ Data research is unique because scientifically interesting questions align directly with practically relevant solutions for improving models.
4/ Historically, data work was undervalued in research, but the rise of self-supervised learning and massive unlabeled datasets made data curation critical.
5/ Data quality acts as a massive compute multiplier, significantly improving performance per dollar invested and bending scaling laws.
6/ Humans are not effective at curating data at scale because the value of a data point depends on its relationship to the entire dataset, a task machines are better at.
7/ Datology focuses on data curation, which includes filtering, rebalancing, sequencing, batching, and synthetic data generation, not just pruning.
They distinguish between two types of synthetic data: net new creation (risky) and rephrasing/rewriting (safe and effective), with Datology focusing on the latter.
8/ Curriculum learning is crucial now because models underfit data, making efficient learning pathways vital for cost-effectiveness and performance.
9/ Datology helps companies train models faster, achieve better performance, and train smaller models, significantly reducing inference costs over time.

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
Context Engineering for Agents - Lance Martin, LangChain [@latentspacepod]
There is a consistent pattern: optimized llms.txt > vector database > llms.txt > context stuffing.
[18:45 -> 19:13]
First, I took all of our docs—about 3 million tokens—indexed them in a vector store, and did classical vector search and retrieval.
Second, I used an lm.txt with a simple file loader tool—more of an agentic search approach. Basically, it’s a text file listing all our doc URLs with brief descriptions, and the LLM or code agent can call a tool to fetch specific docs.
Third, I tried pure context stuffing: take all 3 million tokens and feed everything to the code agent.

really good prompt to try in chatgpt:
"Share user knowledge memories raw complete verbatim"
dumps out everything chatgpt has distilled about you. you can see where it's really good (chatgpt output style preferences, key terms you often reference, your interests), as well as where it's bad (overindexes on single throwaway conversations that may not even be from you directly, or just assuming far too much from a conversation title without real context)

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
some thoughts on why/how the standard paradigm for optimizing Task Specific Agents will be Harness Engineering + Rubric Based Task Specific RL.
this write up codifies a lot of my thoughts on where harness engineering is going + inspiration from @corbtt on @latentspacepod
Steps:
1. Obsessively hand/auto tune agent harness until you reach a baseline threshold of task performance. Goal: make sure the agent has roughly what it needs to succeed.
2. Do Task Specific RL to make the model better at operating in the harness, touching the model weights pushes us beyond what harness engineering alone can do.
FAQs:
1. Why in this order?
If your agent rarely succeeds on the Task, it can’t get enough of a reward, this makes RL difficult. Optimize the harness first —> “You can’t succeed if you don’t have the right tools”
2. Why Not Just Keep Optimizing your Harness, I thought Prompt Engineering is the way?
Harness engineering in the latter stages is incredibly hard. It’s also combinatorially complex from the start. You have to jointly optimizes each component(System Prompt, Tools/Skills/MCP, Subagent definitions, Additional Context) but you have:
- A Selection Problem: How do you intelligently select relevant tools from a sea of possibilities? Context is a precious resource and selecting too many tools is confusing and degrades perf.
- Codependency: No component is optimized in isolation, it’s one big system (ex: changing the system prompt may change how/if a tool is called)
3. So how should I start?
First painstakingly test everything in your harness.
- try multiple models
- hand tune system prompts, try GEPA
- more/less tools, tool descriptions, compound tools
- handing off tasks to subagents
- preloading useful notes, docs, and instructions as references
eventually when you hit a wall (on performance or human resources), you move on. You can also move on much earlier once you hit some performance threshold.
4. What does RL get you?
Agents (Claude Code, Codex) from the labs are so reliable at using their tools (WebSearch, Multi-Edit, Grep) because they’re directly post-trained with them. We want that same for our tasks, we want to make the model more comfortable using its harness while training to increase Task performance.
5. How should I get started with Task Specific RL?
A fantastic first place to start is RULER from @OpenPipeAI which relies on rubrics created by you + LLM as a judge across multiple generations. For your task, you probably already have a set of ideas on what’s good, codifying that in a rubric is all you need to get started
working on writing up a walkthrough blog of this with code. really excited about building products that treat agent building as a harness optimization problem that you measure deeply + push further with RL

summary:
We asked @corbtt about the rise and fall of LoRAs:
“Predicated on the fact that you're doing fine-tuning at all, LoRAs have very, very attractive properties relative to doing a full fine tune, right. Because if you're doing a LoRA, you can at training time.
It makes… It helps some. You're using less memory to train. But it really, where it really helps you out is at inference time. Because if you're doing LoRAs, then when you deploy it for inference, you can multiplex, you know, basically an arbitrarily large number of LoRAs on the same GPU deployment. That lets you do things like per-token pricing as opposed to GPU hour pricing. It just gives you much more flexibility, uh, at deployment time.
I'm actually still a LoRA bull, like for the record. You know, you're talking about the rise and fall. I think LoRAs and you know their future is still out there. Thinking Machines put out like a week or two ago a blog post, doing quite a lot of research on the trade-offs between LoRAs and full fine-tuning in various different training regimes.
I think the reason LoRAs were uncool for a while was mostly just 'cause like fine-tuning was uncool. Like, I think if you're doing fine-tuning anyway, LoRAs are still you know in many cases the way you wanna do it, but not that many people were doing fine-tuning.”

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
我们都希望 AI 助手能真正为我们办事，比如直接预订机票或购买商品。但总有恐惧会阻碍这一切：我真的要把我的信用卡号告诉 ChatGPT 吗？
这正是 Stripe 试图解决的核心问题。
在 @latentspacepod 的最新访谈中，Stripe 的 AI 负责人艾米丽分享了 Stripe 的思考，过去是「人向商家购买」，而现在，「一个智能体坐在了中间」。这个小小的变化，却要求我们从根本上重塑整个金融基础设施。
为什么这么难？艾米丽解释说，这个 AI 助手本身并不想承担风险，它也不想真的经手这笔钱。与此同时，商家（比如航空公司）也希望与最终的消费者建立直接联系，以便处理后续的退款或客服。
这就形成了一个僵局：AI 助手、商家和你，三方都不想（也不该）持有完整的支付风险。
Stripe 与 OpenAI 联手推出的智能体商业协议(Agentic Commerce Protocol)，就是为了解开这个结。它们为此设计了一个叫做共享支付令牌(SharedPaymentToken) 的东西。
请不要把它想象成你的信用卡。你最好把它想象成一个一次性的、高度加密的「任务通行证」。
当你想让 ChatGPT 帮你买东西时，这个系统会生成一个临时的令牌。这个令牌被精确地限定了范围：
- 它只能用于你指定的商家（比如美联航）。
- 它只能用于特定金额上限（比如 500 美元）。
- 它在短时间内就会失效（比如 10 分钟）。
你还可以随时撤销它。
最关键的一点，正如原文所强调的：“底层的凭证（你的真实卡号）永远不会暴露给 AI 智能体。”
AI 助手只是拿着这个临时的通行证去帮你办事。商家收到令牌，通过 Stripe 的系统验证其有效性，然后完成交易。AI 完成了任务，而你的财务信息始终安全地留在保险箱里。
这一个小小的令牌设计，可能是 AI 从一个聊天机器人走向一个商业智能体的关键一步。它在安全和便利之间找到了一个精妙的平衡点，让 AI 真正为我们跑腿变得可能。

Jed Borovik from Google Labs is building Jules, Google’s autonomous coding agent, after nine years working on search. summary:
From a decade building Medal into a 12M-user game clipping platform with billions of highlight moments, Pim turned down a reported $500M offer from OpenAI and raised a $134M seed from Khosla to spin out General Intuition, betting that world models trained on peak human gameplay are the next frontier after LLMs.
We sat down with Pim to dig into why Medal’s clips are “episodic memory for simulation,” how fully vision-based agents that only see pixels can play like (and sometimes better than) humans, transferring from games to real-world video and into robotics, what founders with proprietary data should know before selling or licensing to labs, and his bet that spatial–temporal foundation models will quietly power most real-world AI agents long before anyone calls it AGI.

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
From applied cryptography and offensive security in France’s defense industry to optimizing nuclear submarine workflows, then selling his e-signature startup to Docusign and now running AI as CTO of Superhuman Mail (Superhuman, recently acquired by Grammarly), Loïc Houssier has lived the full arc from deep infra and compliance hell to obsessing over 100ms product experiences and AI-native email.
We sat down with Loïc to dig into how you actually put AI into an inbox without adding latency, why Superhuman leans so hard into agentic search and “Ask AI” over your entire email history, how they design tools vs. agents and fight agent laziness, what box-priced inference and local-first caching mean for cost and reliability, and his bet that your inbox will power your future AI EA while AI massively widens the gap between engineers with real fundamentals and those faking it.

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
From scaling startups in sales and public cloud (including building Palo Alto Networks’ central U.S. cloud business) to joining Kleiner Perkins to help technical founders turn product edge into repeatable revenue, Joubin Mirzadegan built a career around one obsession: distribution. That obsession led him to start the podcast Grit as a hiring wedge, work alongside breakout companies like Glean and Windsurf, and now incubate Roadrunner which is an AI-native rethink of CPQ as SaaS pricing explodes from “seats” into consumption, bundles, renewals, and SKU sprawl.
We sat down with Joubin to dig into the behind-the-scenes craft of great interviews (i.e. why he never sends questions), what Windsurf got right about “Google-class product + Salesforce-class distribution,” how to hire early sales leaders without getting fooled by shiny logos, why legacy CPQ data models are quietly breaking modern revenue teams, and his bet that rebuilding quoting and approvals from the ground up then layering LLMs on top will eliminate the deal-desk Slack chaos and become the backbone for how enterprise AI companies sell in the next decade.

"My favorite definition of sales is an ability to transfer enthusiasm from one person to another. summary:
i *think* i was the first one to refer to this as a "harness" in my o3 pro review for @latentspacepod
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G96zHxhWgAATIm2.jpg
Quoting @_philschmid
If 2025 was beginning of agents, 2026 will be around Agent Harnesses. An Agent Harness is the infrastructure that wraps around an AI model to manage long-running tasks. It is not the agent itself.
It operates at a higher level than agent frameworks. The harness provides prompt presets, opinionated handling for tool calls (Human in the loop), lifecycle hooks or ready-to-use capabilities like planning, filesystem access or sub-agent management.
As Benchmarks are going to become more complex we need to bridge the gap between benchmark claims and user experience. A Agent Harness can be essential for three critical reasons:
- Validating Real-World Progress: Allows users to easily test and compare how the latest models perform against their use cases and constraints.
- Empowering User Experience: Without a harness, the user's experience might be behind the model's potential.
- Hill Climbing via Real-World Feedback: A shared, stable environment (Harness) creates a feedback loop where researchers can iterate and improve ("hill climb") based on actual user adoption.
We are heading toward a convergence of training and inference environments. We see a new bottleneck being context durability. The Harness will become the primary tool for solving "model drift”.

Last month, I dove deep with @swyx on @latentspacepod about the state of context engineering, and scaling it as a full-stack discipline with benchmarks, tooling, and enterprise deployments. Hosted by @LaudeInstitute on the rooftop of the Hard Rock Cafe during @NeurIPSConf (my 5th!), and my first interview in sunglasses! Catch the full video from sunny San Diego here:

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
From a scrappy side project built to solve their own LLM optimization problems to becoming the industry’s de-facto independent scoreboard, Micah Hill-Smith and George Cameron went through the arc of launching Artificial Analysis for free, paying benchmarking costs out of pocket, and growing it into what many now call the “new Gartner of AI” for enterprises, labs, and developers.
We sat down with Micah and George to unpack why truly independent benchmarking is so hard (prompt variance, eval saturation, mystery-shopper policies), how the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index evolved as old benchmarks broke, and what new metrics actually matter now such as agentic evals (GDPVal-AA). We also dig into the economics behind the “smile curve” of AI: why intelligence is getting 100–1000× cheaper per unit while total spend explodes, how reasoning and agents change token efficiency, and their bet that evals must continuously evolve or risk training the industry to optimize for the wrong things.

"The things that get measured become things that get targeted by labs in what they're trying to build.
If you know that you're gonna be graded on a particular thing, if you're a researcher, there are a whole bunch of things that you can do to try to get better at that thing that preferably are going to be helpful for a wide range of how actual users want to use the thing you're building.

Micah discusses the implications of model improvements focusing too much on benchmarks (Goodhart's Law) and how the industry can improve.

summary:
From Palantir and Two Sigma to turning mechanistic interpretability into a production-grade platform, Mark Bissell (Member of Technical Staff) and Myra Deng (Head of Product) are building Goodfire on the belief that “understanding what’s inside the model” is the path to safer, more controllable AI and Goodfire just raised a $150M Series B at a $1.25B valuation to scale that bet.
We sat down with Mark and Myra to unpack what actionable interpretability looks like beyond demos: why SAE features can lose to raw-activation probes on real detection tasks, how they deployed token-level PII monitoring with Rakuten across English + Japanese without training on real customer data, and what it takes to do real-time steering on a trillion-parameter model (including the infamous Gen-Z feature). We also dig into hallucination detection, surgical post-training edits for bias/unlearning, the emerging equivalence between activation steering and in-context learning, and their push to bring interpretability into training so model development isn’t just “data in, weights out.”

From rewriting Google’s search stack in the early 2000s to reviving sparse trillion-parameter models and co-designing TPUs with frontier ML research, Jeff Dean has quietly shaped nearly every layer of the modern AI stack. "Benchmarks, particularly external ones that are publicly available, have their utility, but they often have a lifespan of utility...
I like to think the best kinds of benchmarks are ones where the initial scores are like 10% to 20% or 30% and then you can sort of work on improving that capability and get it up to like 80%, 90%.
I think once it hits kind of ~95%, you get very diminishing returns really focusing on that benchmark because it's either the case that you've now achieved that capability or there's also the issue of leakage in public data or very related kind of data being, being in your training data."

"Even for pre language model-based work, our ranking systems would be built to start with a giant number of web pages in our index, identify a subset of them that are relevant with very lightweight kinds of methods (narrowing down to ~30,000 documents), then apply more and more sophisticated algorithms. summary:
It's time to start tracking this.
open source. we'll maintain the first draft of this special time in history.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCCv2kDbEAAK_v-.jpg
Quoting @karpathy
It is hard to communicate how much programming has changed due to AI in the last 2 months: not gradually and over time in the "progress as usual" way, but specifically this last December. There are a number of asterisks but imo coding agents basically didn’t work before December and basically work since - the models have significantly higher quality, long-term coherence and tenacity and they can power through large and long tasks, well past enough that it is extremely disruptive to the default programming workflow.
Just to give an example, over the weekend I was building a local video analysis dashboard for the cameras of my home so I wrote: “Here is the local IP and username/password of my DGX Spark. Log in, set up ssh keys, set up vLLM, download and bench Qwen3-VL, set up a server endpoint to inference videos, a basic web ui dashboard, test everything, set it up with systemd, record memory notes for yourself and write up a markdown report for me”. The agent went off for ~30 minutes, ran into multiple issues, researched solutions online, resolved them one by one, wrote the code, tested it, debugged it, set up the services, and came back with the report and it was just done. I didn’t touch anything. All of this could easily have been a weekend project just 3 months ago but today it’s something you kick off and forget about for 30 minutes.
As a result, programming is becoming unrecognizable. You’re not typing computer code into an editor like the way things were since computers were invented, that era is over. You're spinning up AI agents, giving them tasks *in English* and managing and reviewing their work in parallel. The biggest prize is in figuring out how you can keep ascending the layers of abstraction to set up long-running orchestrator Claws with all of the right tools, memory and instructions that productively manage multiple parallel Code instances for you. The leverage achievable via top tier "agentic engineering" feels very high right now.
It’s not perfect, it needs high-level direction, judgement, taste, oversight, iteration and hints and ideas. It works a lot better in some scenarios than others (e.g. especially for tasks that are well-specified and where you can verify/test functionality). The key is to build intuition to decompose the task just right to hand off the parts that work and help out around the edges. But imo, this is nowhere near "business as usual" time in software.

A GPT-5.4 rumor was that the model can persist state.
Jeff Dean mentioned this on his @latentspacepod appearance, so clearly something the AI Labs are thinking about.
I'd bet there's a good chance they've discovered how to effectively integrate State-Space Models with Transformers at scale.
SSMs are designed to carry a hidden state forward with every computational step, and scale linearly rather than quadratically like Transformers.
Also backs up the rumor that GPT-5.4 will have a 2 million token context window.
Persistent state would essentially mean that AI models go from being Guy Pearce's character in "Memento" to Dustin Hoffman's character in "Rain Man" overnight.
It would give AI models true long-term memory.
It would be a massive breakthrough for real.

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
Marc Andreessen says if he were 18 right now, AI is "100% what I would be spending all of my time on."
When the co-founder of a16z shares his opinion on what to do in tech, you listen.
When he looks at AI today, he sees something that has never existed before in the history of software.
AI agents can operate with very little human involvement.
The reason is they can run on a Unix shell, the same command line system that has powered computers for decades.
With a single instruction from you, it can access your files, your network, and your devices. Or you can instruct it to rewrite its own code. And even if it needs a new capability, you can allow it to write the code itself and install it.
Here's a real example of this happening:
One of his friends had his agent rewrite the firmware on a robot dog that could barely climb stairs. The agent rebuilt the entire control system. The dog is now a functional pet for his kids, and whenever something breaks, the agent just fixes the code again.
Andreessen says no widely deployed software system in history has ever been able to understand and modify itself like this.
He calls it "an incredible conceptual breakthrough."

@pmarca with @latentspacepod
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2042394665618718722/img/oonaSQTP_jjgsFOh.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2042394665618718722/vid/avc1/480x270/wKzdIKXxpwTVgI2r.mp4?tag=14
Quoting @a16z
"Speed wins."
"You have to be willing to commit to being fast. You can't have long bureaucratic processes. You can't have a risk-averse posture."
@pmarca explains the OODA loop — and why the fastest operator controls the narrative in business, media, and politics:
"There's a framework called the OODA loop, originally developed for fighter pilots and later for broader military strategy."
"It stands for observe, orient, decide, act. It's basically the decision-making cycle."
"If speed is the thing that matters, then the person who gets through that cycle the fastest is the one who's going to win."
"If you can have a sustainably faster OODA loop processing cycle than the next guy — think about what happens… You operate and make a decision within an hour. The other guy is still inside his own OODA loop when you make your decision. He's only halfway through his process and now has to start over. You've changed the parameters of what's going on."
"This is also a big explanation for what's happened in traditional media."
"The New York Times has its own OODA loop, and it's like 24 hours to go through its process."

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
Marc Andreessen says the four most dangerous words in investing are "this time is different."
He's referring to the AI boom.
For 80 years, the field has followed the same pattern.
Excitement builds, money pours in, the technology fails to deliver, and then the industry collapses.
He points to 4 different times:
• In 1943, the original neural network paper was written. It proved that simple mathematical models of brain cells could perform any logical computation. It was a foundational breakthrough but didn't takeoff.
• In 1955, scientists got a grant to spend 10 weeks at Dartmouth and believed they could achieve AGI by the end of the summer. They did not.
• In the 1980s, corporations poured over a billion dollars into "expert systems," AI programs designed to replicate the decision-making of human specialists in medicine, finance, and engineering. By 1987, this entire market crashed.
• In 2016-17, machine learning hype surged again. It faded quickly.
Each time, the technology underdelivered and the money dried up.
But here's what really different about this time.
AI has made four breakthroughs back to back.
1) Language models
2) Reasoning
3) Coding agents
4) Self-improvement
And ALL are generating revenue in production right now.
That's why old Nvidia chips are gaining value instead of depreciating.
And this has literally never happened in computing before.
Every GPU is sold out for the next 3-4 years.
He calls betting against this "essentially suicidal" and "an invitation to get your face ripped off."
He calls it "an 80-year overnight success."
Researchers worked their entire lives on this, and many passed away without seeing it work.
Now it is all arriving at once.
— Marc Andreessen (@pmarca), co-founder at a16z (@a16z) on the Latent Space podcast (@latentspacepod)

summary:
[AINews 14 Apr 2026]
Humanity's Last Gasp
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HF6lZbVasAMTehN.jpg
Quoting @levie
Another week on the road meeting with a couple dozen IT and AI leaders from large enterprises across banking, media, retail, healthcare, consulting, tech, and sports, to discuss agents in the enterprise.
Some quick takeaways:
* Clear that we’re moving from chat era of AI to agents that use tools, process data, and start to execute real work in the enterprise. Complementing this, enterprises are often evolving from “let a thousand flowers bloom” approach to adoption to targeted automation efforts applied to specific areas of work and workflow.
* Change management still will remain one of the biggest topics for enterprises. Most workflows aren’t setup to just drop agents directly in, and enterprises will need a ton of help to drive these efforts (both internally and from partners). One company has a head of AI in every business unit that roles up to a central team, just to keep all the functions coordinated.
* Tokenmaxxing! Most companies operate with very strict OpEx budgets get locked in for the year ahead, so they’re going through very real trade-off discussions right now on how to budget for tokens. One company recently had an idea for a “shark tank” style way of pitching for compute budget. Others are trying to figure out how to ration compute to the best use-cases internally through some hierarchy of needs (my words not theirs).
* Fixing fragmented and legacy systems remain a huge priority right now. Most enterprises are dealing with decades of either on-prem systems or systems they moved to the cloud but that still haven’t been modernized in any meaningful way. This means agents can’t easily tap into these data sources in a unified way yet, so companies are focused on how they modernize these.
* Most companies are *not* talking about replacing jobs due to agents. The major use-cases for agents are things that the company wasn’t able to do before or couldn’t prioritize. Software upgrades, automating back office processes that were constraining other workflows, processing large amounts of documents to get new business or client insights, and so on. More emphasis on ways to make money vs. cut costs.
* Headless software dominated my conversations. Enterprises need to be able to ensure all of their software works across any set of agents they choose. They will kick out vendors that don’t make this technically or economically easy.
* Clear sense that it can be hard to standardize on anything right now given how fast things are moving. Blessing and a curse of the innovation curve right now - no one wants to get stuck in a paradigm that locks them into the wrong architecture. One other result of this is that companies realize they’re in a multi-agent world, which means that interoperability becomes paramount across systems.
* Unanimous sense that everyone is working more than ever before. AI is not causing anyone to do less work right now, and similar to Silicon Valley people feel their teams are the busiest they’ve ever been.
One final meta observation not called out explicitly. It seems that despite Silicon Valley’s sense that AI has made hard things easy, the most powerful ways to use agents is more “technical” than prior eras of software. Skills, MCP, CLIs, etc. may be simple concepts for tech, but in the real world these are all esoteric concepts that will require technical people to help bring to life in the enterprise.
This both means diffusion will take real work and time, but also everyone’s estimation of engineering jobs is totally off. Engineers may not be “writing” software, but they will certainly be the ones to setup and operate the systems that actually automate most work in the enterprise.

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
Notion’s Sarah Sachs & Simon Last on Custom Agents, Evals, and the Futur... via @YouTube
It was such an incredible interview by @latentspacepod with @NotionHQ team's @sarahmsachs & Simon and I recommend everyone building and monetizing agent to listen!
However one little thing keeps popping up in my head. They said that at Notion, before the meeting, a Custom Agent automatically scans all relevant Slack channels and GitHub activity, then generates pre-read materials and shares them with the team. People come into the meeting, read the context, and start the conversation.
After the meeting, the agent integrated with the calendar automatically breaks out the tasks for and sends the agreed follow-up messages in Slack. The people in the meeting do NOT need to take notes or clean things up afterward. They can focus all their energy on the parts that actually require decision-making.
While they revealed that eeting Notes has also become an unexpected growth driver for Notion. I also keep wondering:
Is it 100% good for us to stop taking meeting notes entirely?
🧐 I actually highly doubt that.
A big reason I still try to write down feedback, conversations, and daily reflections in Notion is that the act of writing is not just about record-keeping.
👨‍🏫 It is a process of digestion.
When I write things down myself, I often make new connections and notice patterns. I remember details differently. I turn raw information into something that actually becomes part of my thinking.
If I only read an AI-generated meeting note once, I may understand what happened, but I may not really internalize it.
So while everyone is talking about giving agents better memory, I think there is another question we should not ignore:
What happens if we lose our own memory in the process? If we stop remembering, stop writing, stop reflecting, and our tools are also fragmented across different agents, then what exactly is left for us to contribute?
For me, writing is still one of the most important ways to deepen memory, sharpen judgment, and stay connected to my own thinking.
#Notion #AI

title: Latent.Space (@latentspacepod)
summary:
I just watched an episode of the @latentspacepod podcast with @agarwl_ on LLM distillation.
The video gives a good overview of the different types:
1. Supervised KD
This is the classic Hinton style distillation.
You have teacher logits and train the student to match the teacher probability distribution. For LLMs this means matching next-token probabilities over the vocabulary, usually with forward KL.
This gives the student more information than just the correct token because the teacher distribution contains "dark knowledge".
2. Synthetic data distillation
Here the teacher generates answers and the student is trained on those answers with normal next-token prediction.
This is very practical because you do not need access to teacher logits. API access is enough.
A lot of modern LLM distillation is basically this.
3. Best-of-N distillation
Instead of taking one teacher answer, sample N answers, score them, and train on the best one.
This is especially interesting for reasoning models because the quality of the trajectory matters a lot.
But the video also makes a good point: sometimes many samples from a weaker and cheaper model can beat fewer samples from a stronger expensive model when compute or cost is matched.
4. On-policy distillation / GKD
This was the part that finally clicked for me.
The student generates the trajectory.
Then the teacher is not used to replace the trajectory or just say good or bad.
The teacher scores the student trajectory token-by-token by running a forward pass over prompt + student answer and producing next-token distributions.
So the student learns from the states it actually enters.
This matters because offline distillation has a train-inference mismatch. The student is trained on clean teacher outputs, but at inference time it has to continue from its own mistakes.
On-policy distillation is closer to imitation learning. Let the student drive, then ask the teacher what it would do in the states the student visited.
5. Speculative decoding distillation
The video also connects distillation to speculative decoding.
If a small draft model has token distributions closer to the large target model, the target model accepts more proposed tokens and inference gets faster.
So distillation is not only about making a small standalone model better. It can also make the large model cheaper to serve.

What made LLMs powerful was not just larger models, but training on massive, diverse, naturally occurring data distributions.

• Metagenomics-scale diversity
• Emergent structural understanding
• Latent biological representations

Nature contains an enormous amount of unlabeled biological information that traditional curated datasets have never captured.
Scaling into that space may fundamentally change how biological intelligence is learned.
Another fascinating direction is the use of SAE-style interpretability to uncover internal biological structure representations inside these models.
That raises a stronger possibility:
protein models may eventually become not just predictors, but interpretable biological reasoning systems.

summary:
This recent @latentspacepod pod was a good one (they usually all are).
One specific piece resonated: They were talking about AI agents writing code, and the line was basically that without caution / diligence, your codebase can regress to your worst engineer.
Bad AI-generated code does not just create a one-time cleanup problem. Once it gets into the repo, it becomes part of the context for the next change. The agent sees the bad pattern, assumes it is part of how the system works, and then builds on top of it.
So if you let bad architecture, bad code, or code slop leak into your repo, you are not just making the codebase messier. You are changing the inputs that guide future agent decisions.
This is the failure mode I worry about with coding agents - particularly on larger teams. I get a ton of value out of coding agents, but you need real mechanisms in place to keep them from amplifying the worst parts of your system.
Some of that is technical. You need a system around the agents: better planning, review steps, adversarial agents, fresh-context reviews, tests, checks, and small changes that limit the blast radius. Basically, a team-aligned process around compound engineering.
But that is not enough by itself. You also need experienced people at the wheel.
Especially on a broad team where lots of people have access to these tools, someone still needs to read the code. Someone needs to understand the architecture. Someone needs to know when a change is technically working but pulling the system in the wrong direction.
Bad code in the repo becomes precedent. And once it becomes precedent, the agent can keep building on it until the codebase no longer accurately reflects what you are trying to build - and is hard to move forward, with or without AI agents.
